subtopic_detail: Secondary prevention after a first episode of acute rheumatic fever in a remote community child
stem:
You are the medical officer at a remote clinic in the Northern Territory caring for a nine year old boy admitted three days ago with fever, migrating joint pain and a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Streptococcal serology is rising and the electrocardiogram shows a prolonged PR interval.

The visiting paediatrician has confirmed a first episode of acute rheumatic fever and the echocardiogram shows mild mitral regurgitation. He has completed treatment of the streptococcal infection and his arthritis has settled with naproxen. His mother asks what happens when he goes home.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Soft pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, no carditis symptoms, joints no longer swollen or tender, no subcutaneous nodules and no rash, chest clear on auscultation
data_table.Investigations: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 62 mm/h (0-15), C reactive protein 28 mg/L (less than 5), electrocardiogram shows first degree atrioventricular block, echocardiogram shows mild mitral regurgitation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for ongoing care?

options.text: Give twice daily oral phenoxymethylpenicillin for five years, with pharmacy dose administration aids supplied to the family to support adherence
options.rationale: Daily oral penicillin is the fallback when injections are genuinely refused, because adherence over years is poor and breakthrough recurrences are more frequent than with the injectable form. Convenience aids do not close that gap. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange annual echocardiography and dental review without antibiotics, treating each future sore throat promptly with an appropriate oral agent
options.rationale: Treating only symptomatic pharyngitis misses the many streptococcal infections that are silent or occur in the skin, so recurrences continue. Surveillance detects damage rather than preventing it. (Source: RHDAustralia: ARF and RHD guideline)

options.text: Continue naproxen until the inflammatory markers normalise and start a low dose corticosteroid to protect the mitral valve from further damage
options.rationale: Anti inflammatory treatment relieves arthritis but has never been shown to alter valve outcome, and corticosteroids are reserved for severe carditis with heart failure. Neither prevents the recurrence that drives progressive disease. (Source: RHDAustralia: ARF and RHD guideline)

options.text: Give four weekly intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin, register him with the control program and arrange echocardiographic review
options.rationale: Regular long acting penicillin injections are the only intervention shown to prevent recurrent episodes and progression to established valve disease, and registration ensures recall when the family travels. Echocardiography tracks the valve lesion that determines the duration of prophylaxis. (Source: RHDAustralia: ARF and RHD guideline)

options.text: Give a ten day course of oral phenoxymethylpenicillin now, then review him in the clinic if further sore throats or joint pains develop
options.rationale: A treatment course eradicates the triggering organism but does nothing about the next streptococcal infection, and recurrence is what destroys valves. Primary treatment and secondary prophylaxis are different tasks with different durations. (Source: RHDAustralia: ARF and RHD guideline)

explanation.summary: Acute rheumatic fever remains common in remote parts of northern Australia and carries one of the highest rates of rheumatic heart disease in the world, so recognition and secondary prevention are core Australian practice. Diagnosis uses the Jones criteria with a lowered threshold in high incidence settings, where monoarthritis, polyarthralgia and subclinical carditis on echocardiography all count. Once the diagnosis is made, the intervention that changes the natural history is secondary prophylaxis with four weekly intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin, because each recurrence adds valve damage. Notification and entry onto the jurisdictional control register ensures recall, coordinates delivery across clinics when families move, and tracks echocardiographic severity. Duration depends on age and valve status, continuing for a minimum of ten years or until a defined age, and longer when significant valve disease is present.
key_points: Four weekly intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin is the standard secondary prophylaxis.
Oral penicillin is a second choice used only when injections are refused.
Register notification supports recall and continuity when families move between communities.
Diagnostic criteria are deliberately relaxed in high incidence populations.
Anti inflammatory treatment relieves symptoms but does not protect the valves.
explanation.pearls: Mixing the benzathine injection with lidocaine markedly reduces injection pain without reducing penicillin levels, and pain is the commonest reason young people disengage from a program they need to continue for a decade.

subtopic_detail: Microcytic anaemia in a toddler drinking one and a half litres of cow milk each day
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a two year old girl whose parents think she looks pale in photographs. She is otherwise well, has no bruising and has never passed blood in her stool.

She drinks about one and a half litres of cow milk daily from a bottle, including through the night, and eats little meat or vegetables. She was born at term and her growth has tracked along the twenty fifth centile for weight. Her parents are both Australian born with no family history of anaemia.

data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae and palmar creases, no jaundice, no hepatosplenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, no petechiae or bruising, active and playing normally in the room
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (110-140), mean cell volume 62 fL (75-87), red cell distribution width 19 per cent (11.5-14.5), platelets 480 x10^9/L (150-450), ferritin 6 micrograms/L (20-200), C reactive protein within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reduce the milk intake to about 500 mL daily, start oral iron and recheck the haemoglobin and ferritin after four weeks of treatment
options.rationale: Excessive cow milk displaces iron rich foods, impairs iron absorption and can cause occult gut blood loss, so dietary change and replacement therapy are both required. A four week recheck confirms a response before committing to a full course. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Send coeliac serology with a total immunoglobulin A level and defer any iron treatment until those results have been reviewed in the clinic
options.rationale: Coeliac disease is worth considering when iron deficiency is unexplained, but here the history supplies an ample explanation and the child has no gastrointestinal symptoms or growth faltering. Deferring treatment prolongs a deficiency that affects neurodevelopment. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Refer her to the paediatric haematology clinic for haemoglobin electrophoresis before any dietary or pharmacological treatment is started
options.rationale: A low ferritin with a high red cell distribution width points to deficiency rather than thalassaemia trait, in which ferritin is normal and the cell size is disproportionately small for the degree of anaemia. Electrophoresis performed while iron deplete can also be misleading. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Admit her for a packed red cell transfusion and commence oral iron once the post transfusion haemoglobin has been measured the following morning
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise or cardiac failure, and a playful child who has adapted to slowly developing anaemia does not need it. Rapid transfusion in chronic anaemia risks circulatory overload. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Advise a diet richer in red meat and green vegetables alone, with a repeat full blood count in 3 months to confirm that the anaemia has corrected
options.rationale: Diet alone cannot replenish depleted stores at a useful rate once the ferritin has fallen this low, particularly in a fussy toddler. Dietary advice is an essential adjunct to replacement rather than an alternative. (Source: RACGP: Iron deficiency anaemia in children)
source_refs: RACGP: Iron deficiency anaemia in children

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency is the commonest nutritional deficiency in Australian toddlers and excessive cow milk intake is the usual mechanism, acting through displacement of iron rich solids, inhibition of absorption by calcium and casein, and low grade enteric blood loss. The blood picture shows a microcytic hypochromic anaemia with a high red cell distribution width and a low ferritin, which separates it from thalassaemia trait where ferritin is normal and the red cell count is preserved. Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so a normal value with a raised C reactive protein does not exclude deficiency. Management combines limiting milk to about 500 mL daily with oral iron and a recheck at four weeks, looking for a haemoglobin rise that confirms both the diagnosis and adherence. Treatment continues for about three months after the haemoglobin normalises so that stores are replenished, because neurodevelopmental effects of early deficiency may not be fully reversible.
key_points: Cow milk above about 500 mL daily in a toddler is a leading cause of iron deficiency.
A low ferritin with a high red cell distribution width distinguishes deficiency from thalassaemia trait.
Ferritin rises with inflammation, so interpret it alongside C reactive protein.
Recheck at four weeks to confirm a response before continuing a full course.
Continue iron for about three months beyond normalisation to refill stores.
explanation.pearls: Give oral iron with a vitamin C source and away from milk, and warn families that stools turn black and that teeth can stain temporarily, because these unexpected effects are a common reason treatment is abandoned in the first fortnight.

sources.label: RACGP: Iron deficiency anaemia in children
BMJ Best Practice: Iron deficiency anaemia

subtopic_detail: Fever twelve days after chemotherapy with a neutrophil count of 0.3 in a well looking child
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a six year old girl with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia who is twelve days past her last chemotherapy block. Her mother recorded a temperature of 38.5 degrees Celsius at home an hour ago and brought her straight in, as instructed by the oncology team.

She looks well, is chatting about her dog and has no cough, diarrhoea or dysuria. Her central venous access device site looks clean and is not tender. Her mother mentions that they have a long drive home and asks whether they can wait for the blood results and then leave if everything is reassuring.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and well perfused, mucositis absent, chest clear on auscultation, abdomen soft and not tender, central line exit site clean and dry, no perianal fissure or tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (110-140), white cell count 0.8 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), neutrophils 0.3 x10^9/L (1.5-8.0), platelets 62 x10^9/L (150-450), C reactive protein 42 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Take blood cultures and await the result of the C reactive protein and film review before deciding whether intravenous antibiotics are needed
options.rationale: No laboratory marker reliably separates the child who will become septic from the child who will not, and every hour of delay increases mortality. Risk stratification tools are applied after the first dose, not instead of it. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia)

options.text: Give oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and ciprofloxacin and arrange review in the oncology day unit the following morning for reassessment
options.rationale: Oral regimens are used only in carefully selected low risk children within a defined program, and a neutrophil count this low in the early recovery phase excludes that pathway. Discharge also removes the observation that early deterioration requires. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia)

options.text: Give paracetamol and observe her in the short stay unit for four hours, starting antibiotics only if the fever recurs or she becomes unwell
options.rationale: Antipyretics mask the one sign being used to monitor her and defer the intervention that changes outcome. Fever in neutropenia is treated as an emergency regardless of how the child looks at presentation. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia)

options.text: Arrange a chest radiograph and urine culture first, then start intravenous antibiotics once a focus of infection has been identified on those tests
options.rationale: A focus is found in only a minority of episodes, so requiring one before treating guarantees delay in most children. Imaging is arranged when symptoms point to a site, after antibiotics have been given. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take blood cultures from the central line and a peripheral site and give the first intravenous antibiotic dose within an hour of her arrival
options.rationale: Time to first antibiotic is the modifiable factor most strongly linked to survival in this group, and a well appearance offers no protection because a neutropenic child can decompensate within hours. Cultures are taken alongside rather than before the antibiotic. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile neutropenia)

explanation.summary: Fever with neutropenia in a child receiving chemotherapy is a medical emergency in which the interval between arrival and the first antibiotic dose is the strongest modifiable determinant of outcome, and Australian services audit a target of sixty minutes. The well appearance of the child is a trap rather than reassurance, because neutropenic patients mount few localising signs and can progress from playful to shocked within hours, particularly with gram negative bacteraemia. Blood cultures are taken from each lumen of a central device and from a peripheral vein where possible, but collection must not delay treatment. Empirical therapy covers pseudomonas, usually with an antipseudomonal beta lactam, with an aminoglycoside or a glycopeptide added for shock, known resistant colonisation or a suspected line infection. Investigations for a focus follow the first dose and are directed by symptoms, since no source is identified in most episodes.
key_points: Aim for the first intravenous antibiotic within sixty minutes of arrival.
A well appearance and normal examination do not permit delay.
Cultures are taken from the central device and peripherally, without delaying therapy.
Empirical cover must include pseudomonas.
Inflammatory markers cannot be used to decide whether to treat.
explanation.pearls: A single temperature of 38.5 degrees Celsius, or two readings of 38 degrees Celsius an hour apart, defines fever in this setting, and the perianal region must be inspected but never examined digitally because instrumentation of neutropenic mucosa can seed a bacteraemia.

subtopic_detail: Glucose surveillance at two hours of age in a large for gestational age infant of a diabetic mother
stem:
You are the resident covering the postnatal ward and are asked to review a baby boy born two hours ago at thirty nine weeks weighing 4.35 kg. His mother had gestational diabetes treated with insulin from twenty eight weeks and her glycaemic control in the last month was described as variable.

He had good Apgar scores, went to the breast within the first half hour and fed for about ten minutes. He is now asleep in the cot beside his mother, is pink and warm, and the midwife has not yet taken any blood glucose measurement. His mother is keen to avoid formula if possible.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138 beats per minute, blood pressure not recorded, respiratory rate 48 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Well grown and plethoric, moving all four limbs, no jitteriness at rest, anterior fontanelle soft, no respiratory distress, suck strong when offered a finger

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his glucose?

options.text: Measure the blood glucose just before the next feed and follow the newborn hypoglycaemia pathway, supporting frequent feeding in the meantime
options.rationale: Infants of diabetic mothers have hyperinsulinaemia and are screened routinely, with the first sample taken before a feed at two to four hours of age rather than in the immediate postnatal nadir. Feeding support in the interval is part of the same pathway. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Measure the blood glucose only if he becomes jittery, feeds poorly or has an abnormal cry, since he is currently well and has already fed at the breast
options.rationale: Symptom triggered testing misses the substantial proportion of affected babies who are asymptomatic until they seize, which is precisely why risk factor based screening exists. Clinical signs are neither sensitive nor specific in the newborn. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Measure the blood glucose immediately, and if it is below the treatment threshold transfer him to the special care nursery for an intravenous infusion
options.rationale: A sample in the first hour or two captures the physiological nadir that all newborns pass through and generates unnecessary intervention. Escalation to intravenous dextrose follows failure of feeding and buccal gel rather than a single early value. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Give a formula top up after each breastfeed for the first day and measure the blood glucose once daily while he remains on the postnatal ward
options.rationale: Routine supplementation undermines breastfeeding without addressing the monitoring requirement, and daily sampling is far too infrequent for the first twenty four hours. Supplementation is reserved for documented low values or inadequate feeding. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Clinical information)

options.text: Give buccal dextrose gel now as prophylaxis against hypoglycaemia and measure the blood glucose six hours after birth with the routine observations
options.rationale: Dextrose gel is treatment for a documented low value alongside a feed, and prophylactic use in an unscreened baby is not established practice. Deferring the first measurement to six hours leaves the highest risk window unmonitored. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Infants of mothers with diabetes are hyperinsulinaemic at birth because fetal islet hypertrophy persists after the maternal glucose supply is cut off, and macrosomia is the visible marker of that exposure. Australian pathways screen these babies along with those who are small or large for gestational age, preterm or unwell, taking the first capillary glucose before a feed at around two to four hours of age. Sampling earlier than this captures the normal postnatal nadir and prompts intervention that the baby does not need, while waiting for symptoms misses the many infants who remain asymptomatic until they have a seizure. Management escalates from early and frequent feeding, to buccal dextrose gel given with a feed for values below the threshold, to intravenous dextrose when values remain low or the baby is symptomatic. Screening continues through several pre feed measurements until values are consistently satisfactory.
key_points: Macrosomia in a diabetic pregnancy signals fetal hyperinsulinaemia and hypoglycaemia risk.
The first glucose is taken before a feed at about two to four hours, not immediately after birth.
Asymptomatic hypoglycaemia is common, so symptom triggered testing is unsafe.
Buccal dextrose gel with a feed is the first line treatment for a low value.
Screening continues over several pre feed samples before it can be stopped.
explanation.pearls: Persisting hypoglycaemia beyond the first two or three days, or a glucose requirement above eight milligrams per kilogram per minute, is no longer explained by maternal diabetes and calls for a formal hypoglycaemia screen with insulin, cortisol and ketones drawn while the glucose is low.

subtopic_detail: Jitteriness and poor feeding on day three in the baby of a mother on methadone maintenance
stem:
You are the resident on the postnatal ward asked to see a three day old girl who is unsettled between feeds. Her mother is on a stable methadone program and has been engaged with the drug and alcohol service throughout the pregnancy.

The baby was born at thirty eight weeks weighing 2.9 kg and has been rooming in. The midwives report a high pitched cry, difficulty settling after feeds and three loose stools today. She is breastfeeding with some difficulty maintaining attachment. Her temperature and the rest of her observations have remained normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 162 beats per minute, blood pressure not recorded, respiratory rate 58 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tremulous when disturbed and settling when swaddled, increased tone in the limbs, excoriation over the nose from rubbing, no fever, anterior fontanelle soft, weight 2.78 kg today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral morphine now at a weight based dose and wean it over the following week, continuing to room in with her mother on the ward
options.rationale: Pharmacological treatment is reserved for babies whose scores cross a defined threshold on repeated assessments, because many settle with environmental measures alone. Treating early commits the pair to a longer admission without benefit. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

options.text: Advise that breastfeeding be replaced with formula to remove ongoing drug exposure, and observe her on the ward for a further forty eight hours
options.rationale: Breastfeeding is encouraged for women on stable opioid substitution because the amount transferred is small and feeding reduces the severity and duration of withdrawal. Stopping it abruptly can worsen symptoms. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Clinical information)

options.text: Give a dose of naloxone to clarify whether the symptoms are opioid related, then observe her closely in the nursery for the rest of the day
options.rationale: Naloxone precipitates acute withdrawal and seizures in an opioid exposed newborn and is contraindicated in this setting. There is no diagnostic role for it here. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion

options.text: Perform a full septic screen including lumbar puncture and start intravenous antibiotics while awaiting culture results in the special care nursery
options.rationale: Sepsis must be considered when a newborn deteriorates, but this baby is afebrile with normal perfusion and a clinical picture explained by the known exposure. Reflex septic screening separates mother and baby and undermines feeding. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

options.text: Begin structured withdrawal scoring with supportive non pharmacological care, and start medication if the scores remain above the treatment threshold
options.rationale: Scoring on a validated tool at set intervals is what distinguishes an unsettled baby from one who needs opioid replacement, and swaddling, low stimulus care and frequent feeds resolve many cases without medication. Treatment decisions follow consecutive scores rather than a single impression. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

explanation.summary: Neonatal abstinence syndrome after intrauterine opioid exposure typically appears within the first three days for heroin and later, up to about a week, for methadone because of its longer half life. Assessment uses a structured scoring tool such as the Finnegan or its modified versions, applied at consistent intervals after feeds, and the decision to medicate rests on consecutive scores above threshold rather than on a single observation. Non pharmacological care is the foundation of treatment and includes rooming in, swaddling, minimal handling and light, frequent feeding, and dedicated units achieve lower medication rates with these measures. When medication is needed, oral morphine is the usual first agent, with phenobarbitone added for polydrug exposure. Breastfeeding is supported for women on stable opioid substitution because it reduces the severity and duration of withdrawal, and naloxone is contraindicated because it precipitates abrupt withdrawal and seizures.
key_points: Methadone exposed babies may not show peak withdrawal until several days after birth.
Structured repeated scoring drives the decision to medicate.
Rooming in, swaddling and frequent feeds reduce the need for medication.
Breastfeeding is encouraged on stable opioid substitution therapy.
Naloxone is contraindicated because it precipitates acute withdrawal.
explanation.pearls: Score after a feed rather than during a period of hunger, because a hungry baby scores as irritable and excessively sucking, and inconsistent timing of scoring is the commonest reason infants are started on morphine they do not need.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion

subtopic_detail: Six cafe au lait macules with axillary freckling in a seven year old with a normal examination
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a seven year old boy whose mother has noticed more brown patches on his skin over the past two years. He is well, is progressing normally at school and has no headaches or visual complaints.

His father has similar skin patches and was told as a child that they were harmless birthmarks. On examination the boy has six flat light brown macules on the trunk and limbs, each more than five millimetres across, together with freckling in both axillae. His growth is on the fiftieth centile and the rest of the examination is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Six flat light brown macules over 5 mm on trunk and limbs, freckling in both axillae, no palpable cutaneous nodules, no scoliosis, visual acuity 6/6 in each eye, no proptosis, neurological examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing plan?

options.text: Order genetic testing of the responsible gene and defer any surveillance or referral until a pathogenic variant has been demonstrated in the child
options.rationale: Molecular testing is useful for atypical presentations and reproductive counselling but is not needed when clinical criteria are met, and awaiting it delays surveillance. A negative result would not overturn a clinical diagnosis. (Source: Genetics Services Australia: Neurofibromatosis)

options.text: Arrange annual review including ophthalmology assessment, blood pressure measurement and examination of the spine, with referral to genetics
options.rationale: The skin findings meet the diagnostic criteria in a child with an affected parent, and annual surveillance targets the complications that matter, namely optic pathway glioma, hypertension from renal artery or adrenal disease, and scoliosis. Genetics involvement supports family counselling. (Source: RCH CPG: Neurofibromatosis type 1)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits now to screen for an optic pathway lesion, and review him once the scan is reported
options.rationale: Routine neuroimaging of asymptomatic children is not recommended, because incidental findings are common and lesions that matter declare themselves through visual or endocrine change. Imaging is triggered by abnormal ophthalmological assessment or new symptoms. (Source: RCH CPG: Neurofibromatosis type 1)

options.text: Refer him for a skin biopsy of one of the pigmented lesions to confirm the diagnosis before organising any long term surveillance arrangements
options.rationale: The diagnosis is clinical and a biopsy of a pigmented macule adds nothing to criteria that are already satisfied. It also subjects a child to a procedure whose result cannot change management. (Source: RCH CPG: Neurofibromatosis type 1)

options.text: Reassure the family that the pigmented patches are inherited birthmarks like his father's, and review him only if new symptoms develop
options.rationale: Six macules of this size with axillary freckling is a recognised diagnostic combination rather than a benign familial pattern, and the father is most likely affected too. Discharging the child forfeits surveillance during the years when optic glioma presents. (Source: RCH CPG: Neurofibromatosis type 1)

explanation.summary: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is diagnosed clinically when two or more criteria are present, and the combination most often seen in a young child is six or more cafe au lait macules over five millimetres with skinfold freckling in the axillae or groin. Other criteria include two or more neurofibromas or one plexiform neurofibroma, two or more Lisch nodules, optic pathway glioma, a characteristic bony lesion such as sphenoid dysplasia or tibial pseudarthrosis, and an affected first degree relative. Cutaneous neurofibromas usually appear around puberty, so their absence in a seven year old is expected and does not argue against the diagnosis. Surveillance is annual and clinical, covering vision and ophthalmological assessment for optic pathway glioma, blood pressure for renal artery stenosis and phaeochromocytoma, growth and puberty for hypothalamic involvement, the spine for scoliosis, and learning and behaviour, which are the commonest day to day problems. Routine imaging of asymptomatic children is not recommended.
key_points: Two or more diagnostic criteria establish the diagnosis clinically.
Six or more cafe au lait macules with skinfold freckling is the usual childhood combination.
Cutaneous neurofibromas typically appear around puberty and are not expected earlier.
Annual surveillance covers vision, blood pressure, growth, spine and learning.
Routine brain imaging in asymptomatic children is not indicated.
explanation.pearls: Measure the blood pressure at every visit, because hypertension in a child with this condition is renal artery stenosis or phaeochromocytoma until proven otherwise rather than essential hypertension, and it is easily missed when the cuff is skipped in a well looking child.
